questions.question: What is Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection (DI) in Spring?
questions.title: Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection in Spring
questions.direct_answer: IoC is the design principle where the framework — not your code — controls object creation and lifecycle. Dependency Injection is the mechanism Spring uses to implement IoC: dependencies are provided to a class from the outside rather than created internally. This decoupling is what makes Spring applications testable, configurable, and loosely coupled.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate distinguishes the principle (IoC) from the mechanism (DI) and can articulate why this matters beyond textbook definitions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating IoC and DI as synonyms — IoC is the broad principle (framework calls you, not you calling the framework), DI is one specific way to achieve it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why constructor injection is preferred over field injection: it makes dependencies explicit, enforces immutability, and allows unit testing without a Spring context.

sections.title: The `new` Keyword Is a Hard Dependency — and IoC Is Spring's Answer
sections.content:
Every Java tutorial shows the same starting point: a service class that creates its dependencies with `new`. `OrderService` doing `new StripeGateway()` inside its constructor couples the two classes permanently — swap payment providers, write a unit test, or deploy to staging and you're editing `OrderService` every time. The `new` keyword isn't just syntax; it's a hard dependency on a specific implementation.

**Inversion of Control** (IoC) is Spring's answer to this. Instead of your class reaching out to create its dependencies, the framework controls object creation and lifecycle. Your class declares what it needs — Spring decides how, when, and with which implementation to provide it. This is the Hollywood Principle: "Don't call us, we'll call you." Spring's `ApplicationContext` is the IoC container: it reads your `@Component`, `@Service`, and `@Bean` declarations, instantiates beans, resolves their dependencies, and manages the full lifecycle from creation to destruction.

**Dependency Injection** (DI) is the specific mechanism Spring uses to implement IoC. Instead of `OrderService` calling `new StripeGateway()`, Spring injects a `PaymentGateway` implementation through the constructor. The class depends on an interface, not a concrete type. Spring provides `StripeGateway` in production, `SandboxGateway` in staging, and a mock in tests — and `OrderService` never changes.

The distinction interviewers probe: **IoC is the principle, DI is one mechanism to achieve it.** Service Locator is another IoC mechanism — the class asks a registry for dependencies. DI inverts even that: the container pushes dependencies in without the class asking. Spring uses DI. Knowing this difference — and explaining the `new` keyword cost with a concrete example — is what separates a textbook answer from a production-aware one.

sections.title: The `new` Keyword Trap: One Coupling, Four Problems
Constructor Injection: Declare the Need, Let Spring Fulfill It
Constructor vs Setter vs Field Injection: The Differences That Matter
sections.content:
The three injection styles look like alternatives. They're not equally valid for mandatory dependencies. The rows that matter most: `final` fields (immutability), unit testability without Spring, and how circular dependencies are surfaced.

| | Constructor | Setter | Field |
|---|---|---|---|
| `final` fields | Yes | No | No |
| Unit testable without Spring | Yes — `new Foo(dep)` | Yes — `foo.setDep(dep)` | No — reflection required |
| Dependencies visible | Yes — constructor signature | Yes — setter method | No — hidden `@Autowired` |
| For mandatory deps | Yes | No | Either |
| For optional deps | No | Yes | Either |
| Circular dep detection | Startup — `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` | Runtime | Runtime |
| `@Autowired` required | No (single ctor, Spring 4.3+) | Yes | Yes |
| Spring team stance | Preferred | Optional deps only | Discouraged |

The circular dependency row is the most interview-relevant. Constructor injection surfaces the design problem at startup — fail fast, fix early. Field injection hides it until runtime through partially-initialized proxies.

sections.title: Three Things Constructor Injection Gets Right That the Others Don't
When Spring Injects — and Why @Autowired Fields Are Null in the Constructor
sections.content:
Spring resolves dependencies at different points depending on the injection style, and the timing difference causes the most common Spring debugging session for developers mixing injection styles.

**Constructor injection** resolves dependencies before the object exists. Spring builds the full dependency graph, determines instantiation order, and passes all required beans as constructor arguments. The object is fully wired from the first line of the constructor body — no partially-initialized state is possible.

**Field and setter injection** happen after the object is created. The bean is instantiated first (no-arg constructor), then `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` runs in the `postProcessProperties` phase, using `Field.setAccessible(true)` to write into private fields. This is why an `@Autowired` field read inside the constructor returns `null` — the post-processor hasn't run yet. Move that initialization logic to `@PostConstruct`.

This timing difference explains the circular dependency behavior interviewers probe. With constructor injection, Spring must resolve A before creating B and B before creating A — an impossibility caught at startup with `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`. With field injection, Spring creates A (uninitialized), creates B, injects A into B, then finishes A — hiding the cycle through partially-initialized beans.

For optional dependencies, avoid `@Autowired(required = false)` — it silently injects `null` and propagates NPE risk to every call site. The better approach: `private final Optional<MetricsService> metricsService` — Spring wraps the result, optionality is explicit in the type, and there's no NPE risk.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **IoC ≠ DI** — IoC is the principle (framework controls lifecycle, not your class); DI is one mechanism. Service Locator is another — in DI, the container pushes dependencies in without the class asking.
- **Spring 4.3+: no `@Autowired` on single-constructor classes** — Spring uses the sole constructor automatically. Add `@RequiredArgsConstructor` (Lombok) + `private final` fields for zero-boilerplate constructor injection.
- **Constructor injection = startup failure for circular deps** — `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at boot. Field/setter injection hides circular deps until runtime via partially-initialized proxy beans.
- **`@Autowired` fields are `null` in the constructor body** — `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` fires after construction, not during. Reading field-injected deps in the constructor causes NPE; move logic to `@PostConstruct`.
- **`Optional<T>` over `@Autowired(required = false)`** — `Optional<MetricsService>` makes optionality explicit in the type; `required = false` silently injects `null` and propagates NPE risk to every call site.
- **`final` = JVM-guaranteed immutability** — constructor-injected `final` fields are set once, safe across threads. Field injection cannot use `final`. Immutable beans eliminate a class of threading bugs common in shared singleton state.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring's whole model is built around one insight — the `new` keyword is a hard dependency. When `OrderService` does `new StripeGateway()` inside its constructor, those two classes are permanently coupled. You can't swap the gateway, test in isolation, or configure differently per environment without modifying `OrderService`. IoC and Dependency Injection are Spring's solution to that problem.

**Inversion of Control**
- IoC means the framework controls object creation and lifecycle — your class doesn't reach out and wire itself
- Spring's `ApplicationContext` is the IoC container: it reads your `@Component` and `@Bean` declarations, creates beans, resolves dependencies, and manages their lifecycle
- The shift: you declare what you need, Spring decides which implementation to provide based on what's registered

**Dependency Injection**
- DI is the specific mechanism — dependencies come in from outside the class (constructor, setter, or field) instead of being created internally with `new`
- This is what makes testing clean: `new OrderService(mockGateway)` in a unit test, `StripeGateway` in production — `OrderService` never changes
- IoC and DI are not synonyms: IoC is the principle, DI is one mechanism. Service Locator is another IoC pattern — in DI, the container pushes dependencies in; the class doesn't ask for them

**Constructor injection**
- The Spring team's recommendation for mandatory dependencies: `final` fields, explicit constructor signature, testable without the container
- Since Spring 4.3, a class with one constructor doesn't need `@Autowired` — Spring uses it automatically. Add Lombok's `@RequiredArgsConstructor` and you get zero-boilerplate injection
- The practical tell: constructor injection exposes circular dependencies at startup (`BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`). Field injection hides them and produces partially-initialized proxy beans that fail only at runtime

Field injection looks cleaner — one `@Autowired` per field — but you can't unit test without Spring, dependencies are invisible, and `final` is impossible. In modern Spring projects, constructor injection for mandatory deps and setter injection for optional ones is the standard. Field injection is a legacy pattern worth moving away from.

questions.question: What are the differences between constructor injection, field injection, and setter injection?
questions.title: Constructor Injection vs Field Injection vs Setter Injection
questions.direct_answer: Constructor injection wires dependencies through the constructor, making them final and available immediately — it is the Spring team's recommended approach. Field injection uses @Autowired on fields directly (convenient but not testable without a container). Setter injection uses @Autowired on setter methods, allowing optional or re-injectable dependencies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of testability trade-offs and the reasoning behind the Spring team's preference for constructor injection.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking all three are equivalent for production use; not knowing that field injection hides circular dependencies and makes unit testing harder.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that constructor injection exposes circular dependencies at startup (Spring throws a BeanCurrentlyInCreationException) rather than hiding them, and that it enables immutable design with final fields.

sections.title: Why the Spring Team Picked a Winner — and Most Codebases Still Get It Wrong
sections.content:
The three injection styles aren't equally valid alternatives — they represent a **spectrum from explicit to hidden dependency management**, and the choice has consequences for testability, immutability, and how fast design problems surface.

**Constructor injection** wires dependencies at object creation time. The constructor parameter list is the class's contract — every collaborator is visible, fields can be `final`, and you can test with plain `new` and mocks. No Spring context, no reflection. This is why the Spring team officially recommends it for all mandatory dependencies.

**Field injection** uses `@Autowired` directly on private fields. It looks clean — no constructor boilerplate — but the simplicity is deceptive. Dependencies are invisible from outside the class, `final` is impossible, and testing requires either `ReflectionTestUtils` or a full Spring context. Worse, it hides design problems: a class with 12 field-injected dependencies looks tidy while violating Single Responsibility.

**Setter injection** lives in the middle. Dependencies are visible via method signatures and settable in tests, but they can't be `final` and require null-checks since they might not be called. The legitimate use case is optional dependencies — collaborators that enhance behavior but aren't required for the class to function.

sections.title: The Three Styles Compared: When Each Matters and What Breaks
sections.content:
The key rows are **injection timing**, finality, and circular dependency behavior — those drive the practical trade-offs that interviewers probe.

| Aspect | Constructor Injection | Field Injection | Setter Injection |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spring annotation | None required (single ctor) or @Autowired | @Autowired on field | @Autowired on setter |
| Injection timing | During construction | After construction (BeanPostProcessor) | After construction |
| Field can be final | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | ❌ No |
| Unit testable w/o Spring | ✅ Yes (new Foo(dep)) | ❌ No (reflection required) | ✅ Yes (call setter) |
| Mandatory vs optional | ✅ Enforces mandatory | ⚠️ Hard to enforce | ✅ Good for optional |
| Circular dependency | ❌ Fails at startup | ✅ Resolved by Spring | ✅ Resolved by Spring |
| Exposes large ctor smell | ✅ Yes (good signal) | ❌ Hidden | ❌ Partially hidden |
| Spring recommendation | ✅ Preferred | ❌ Discouraged | ⚠️ For optional deps |

sections.title: The Lombok Shortcut and Why Kotlin Gets Constructor Injection for Free
sections.content:
In practice, most Spring teams use **Lombok's `@RequiredArgsConstructor`** to eliminate constructor boilerplate while keeping `final` fields. The annotation generates a constructor for every `final` field, giving you the benefits of constructor injection without writing the constructor yourself.

This works because Spring 4.3+ automatically uses the **sole constructor** of a class for injection — no `@Autowired` annotation needed. A class with `@RequiredArgsConstructor` and three `final` fields gets a three-argument constructor that Spring discovers and invokes automatically.

Kotlin takes this further. Spring treats Kotlin **primary constructors** identically to Java constructor injection. A Kotlin class `class OrderService(private val gateway: PaymentGateway)` is constructor-injected without any annotations at all. The `val` keyword makes the field `final` by default, and the primary constructor is the only constructor, so Spring resolves it automatically. This is why the testability story is identical across JVM languages — constructor injection is a design pattern, not a Java-specific trick.

questions.question: How does @Autowired work internally? What role does BeanPostProcessor and reflection play?
questions.title: How @Autowired Works Internally
questions.direct_answer: @Autowired is processed by AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, which uses Java reflection to scan each bean's fields, setters, and constructors for the annotation. It then queries the BeanFactory to resolve matching beans by type — and by name if there is ambiguity — before injecting them via reflection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of the container's wiring mechanism and when injection actually occurs relative to the constructor.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @Autowired is magic syntax; not knowing it fires after object construction, making field injection unavailable in the constructor body.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how @Autowired on a constructor skips the field-injection phase entirely and why that makes constructor injection more testable.

sections.title: Why @Autowired Isn't Magic — It's a BeanPostProcessor Running Reflection
sections.content:
Most developers treat `@Autowired` as compiler magic — annotate a field, and Spring somehow fills it in. The reality is a **concrete processing pipeline** that runs after the object is constructed, and understanding it explains why field-injected dependencies are `null` inside the constructor and why constructor injection behaves fundamentally differently.

The key player is `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, a `BeanPostProcessor` that Spring registers automatically when you use `@SpringBootApplication` or `<context:annotation-config/>`. It scans every bean class for `@Autowired`, `@Value`, and JSR-330's `@Inject` annotations, builds a list of injection points, and resolves each one from the `BeanFactory`.

The timing distinction matters. **Constructor injection** resolves dependencies before the object exists — Spring looks up the required beans, then passes them as constructor arguments. The object is fully wired from the first line of the constructor body. **Field and setter injection** happen after construction — the `BeanPostProcessor` fires during the `postProcessProperties` phase, using `Field.setAccessible(true)` to bypass `private` modifiers and write directly into the field. This is why an `@Autowired` field is `null` if you read it inside the constructor — the post-processor hasn't run yet.

sections.title: How Spring Finds Injection Points Before Any Bean Exists
sections.content:
Before Spring creates any bean instance, it parses every `@Component`-annotated class into a `BeanDefinition` — a metadata object that describes the class name, scope, constructor arguments, and dependencies. During this phase, `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` inspects the class for injection metadata.

The processor scans three locations: **constructors** annotated with `@Autowired` (or the sole constructor in Spring 4.3+), **fields** with `@Autowired` or `@Value`, and **methods** with `@Autowired`. For each discovered injection point, it creates an `InjectionMetadata` object that caches the target `Field` or `Method` reference and the required type.

This metadata is cached per bean class, so the reflection scan happens only once per type — even for prototype-scoped beans that are instantiated many times. The caching is important because Java reflection has real overhead: `Class.getDeclaredFields()` and `Class.getDeclaredMethods()` are not free operations, and calling them on every bean creation would add visible startup cost in large applications with thousands of beans.

sections.title: Type Resolution: What Happens When Multiple Beans Match
sections.content:
When `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` resolves an injection point, it asks the `BeanFactory` for all beans matching the declared type. The resolution follows a **strict fallback chain** that determines which bean gets injected.

**Step 1 — Type match.** Spring searches the registry for all beans assignable to the injection point's type. If exactly one match exists, it's injected immediately.

**Step 2 — Qualifier narrowing.** If multiple beans match the type, Spring checks for `@Qualifier("name")` on the injection point. If present, only the bean with the matching qualifier survives.

**Step 3 — Primary selection.** Without a qualifier, Spring looks for a bean marked `@Primary`. If exactly one primary exists among the candidates, it wins.

**Step 4 — Name fallback.** As a last resort, Spring compares the **field or parameter name** against bean names. If you have `private PaymentGateway stripeGateway`, Spring will match a bean named `stripeGateway` if no qualifier or primary resolved the ambiguity.

If none of these steps produce a single winner, Spring throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` at startup. This fail-fast behavior is deliberate — ambiguous injection is always a configuration error, not something to resolve silently.

sections.title: The Reflection Call: How Field.setAccessible(true) Bypasses Private Modifiers
sections.content:
For field injection, the actual wiring happens through Java reflection. The `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` calls `Field.setAccessible(true)` on the private field — this is the JVM's mechanism for bypassing access modifiers — and then calls `Field.set(bean, resolvedDependency)` to write the dependency directly into the field.

This is why field injection cannot work with `final` fields. Java's `final` field semantics guarantee that the value is set exactly once during construction. Reflection can technically write to a `final` field, but the JVM is allowed to inline the original value, meaning the write might not be visible to other code. The Java Memory Model makes this behavior **undefined**, which is why Spring doesn't attempt it.

Constructor injection sidesteps this entirely. Dependencies are resolved before the constructor runs and passed as arguments — no reflection on fields, no access modifier tricks. The resulting fields can be `final`, the object is fully immutable after construction, and the entire process is transparent to the JVM's optimization pipeline. This fundamental difference in the injection mechanism — constructor arguments vs reflective field writes — is what makes constructor injection the Spring team's recommended approach.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` — not magic, a BeanPostProcessor** — it's a concrete post-processor Spring registers automatically; it scans every bean for `@Autowired`, `@Value`, and `@Inject` then resolves and injects them.
- **Field-injected deps are `null` in the constructor body** — the BeanPostProcessor fires in `postProcessProperties`, after the constructor returns; reading an `@Autowired` field inside the constructor causes NPE.
- **Resolution order: type → `@Qualifier` → `@Primary` → field name** — Spring walks this fallback chain; if nothing resolves to exactly one bean, `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` fails startup.
- **`Field.setAccessible(true)` bypasses `private` — `final` is impossible** — reflection writes past access modifiers; the JVM's memory model leaves reflective writes to `final` fields as undefined behavior, so field injection can never use `final`.
- **Injection metadata is cached per class, not per instance** — the `Class.getDeclaredFields()` scan runs once per bean type; prototype beans created thousands of times pay the reflection cost only once.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When you annotate a field with `@Autowired`, Spring doesn't touch the compiler — it delegates to a `BeanPostProcessor` that runs after your object is constructed and uses Java reflection to write into private fields. That's the whole mechanism.

**The processor**
- `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` is registered automatically with `@SpringBootApplication`; it scans every bean class for `@Autowired`, `@Value`, and `@Inject`
- For constructor injection, this step is skipped — dependencies are resolved before the object exists and passed as arguments
- For field and setter injection, the processor fires in `postProcessProperties`, after the constructor returns — which is why `@Autowired` fields read inside a constructor body return `null`

**Type resolution**
- Spring searches for matching beans by type first; if exactly one matches, it is injected immediately
- With multiple type matches: `@Qualifier` narrows by name, `@Primary` picks the default, and field name is the last resort — none of these resolve to one? `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` fails startup

**The reflection call**
- `Field.setAccessible(true)` bypasses `private` modifiers; `Field.set(bean, resolvedDependency)` writes the value directly
- This is why field injection cannot use `final` — the JVM's memory model leaves reflective writes to `final` fields undefined; constructor injection avoids this entirely
- Injection metadata is cached per class so the reflection scan runs once per type, not once per prototype instance

Understanding this chain — BeanPostProcessor, type resolution, reflection — explains most of the my `@Autowired` is not working debugging sessions. Constructor injection sidesteps all of it.

sections.title: When Spring Finds Two Beans of the Same Type — and How @Qualifier and @Primary Break the Tie
sections.content:
The most common Spring startup error in any non-trivial application is `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` — Spring found multiple beans of the same type and doesn't know which one to inject. This happens naturally as applications grow: you add a second `DataSource` for a reporting database, a second `RestTemplate` with different timeouts, or a second `PaymentGateway` implementation for a new provider.

Spring's default behavior is strict — **if exactly one bean matches the required type, it's injected. If two or more match, Spring refuses to guess.** This fail-fast approach is deliberate: silently picking one would create bugs that only surface in production.

`@Primary` and `@Qualifier` are the two disambiguation mechanisms. **`@Primary` marks a default** — the bean Spring should choose when no other guidance is given. `@Qualifier` is explicit selection — the injection point names exactly which bean it wants. When both are present, `@Qualifier` wins because it's more specific. Understanding this precedence chain — and knowing that the field name itself is the last-resort fallback — is what interviewers are testing.

sections.title: How @Primary Sets the Default and @Qualifier Overrides It
The Field Name Fallback and Why Custom Qualifier Annotations Scale Better
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Qualifier` > `@Primary` > field name — resolution order matters** — when `@Qualifier` is present at the injection point, `@Primary` is completely ignored; field name is the silent last resort and breaks when you rename the variable.
- **`@Qualifier` value = bean name, lowercase first letter** — `@Qualifier("SmsNotifier")` fails at startup; the default bean name is the class name with a lowercase first character (`smsNotifier`); `@Component("customName")` overrides this.
- **`@Primary` on two beans of the same type results in `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`** — Spring does not pick between two primaries; it fails fast at startup.
- **Custom `@Qualifier` annotations = compile-time safety** — string-based `@Qualifier("stripe")` fails only at runtime on a typo; a `@Stripe` meta-annotation catches typos at compile time and survives refactoring.
- **Field name fallback is silent and fragile** — `private Notifier smsNotifier` matches a bean named `smsNotifier` without any annotation; rename the field and injection silently breaks.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When Spring finds multiple beans of the same type, it refuses to guess which one to inject — `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` at startup. `@Primary` and `@Qualifier` are the two tools that break the tie, and they follow a clear precedence order.

**`@Primary`**
- Marks the default candidate — any injection point that asks for `Notifier` by type gets `EmailNotifier` without needing a qualifier
- When `@Qualifier` is also present at the injection point, `@Qualifier` wins — it is more specific and completely overrides `@Primary`
- Putting `@Primary` on two beans of the same type does not resolve the ambiguity — Spring throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` again

**`@Qualifier`**
- Provides explicit selection at the injection point — names exactly which bean is wanted
- The value must match the bean name exactly, lowercase first letter — `@Qualifier("SmsNotifier")` produces a `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`, not a type-match failure
- Custom qualifier annotations are type-safe: `@Stripe PaymentGateway gateway` — typos fail at compile time, not at deployment

The field name is Spring's last-resort fallback — declare `private Notifier smsNotifier` and Spring matches a bean named `smsNotifier` without any annotation. It works, but rename the field and injection silently breaks. Custom qualifier annotations are the production-ready approach for codebases with multiple implementations of the same interface.

questions.title: @Value and Property Injection — Externalized Configuration
questions.question: How does @Value work for injecting properties into Spring beans?

sections.title: Why Missing Properties Crash Your Application — and the One-Character Fix
sections.content:
`@Value` is the simplest way to get external configuration into a Spring bean — and it's also the most common source of startup failures for teams that don't know one syntax detail. When you write `@Value("${api.url}")` and `api.url` isn't defined in any property source, Spring doesn't inject null or an empty string. It throws `IllegalArgumentException` and your application refuses to start.

The fix is a single colon: `@Value("${api.url:}")` provides an empty string default. `@Value("${api.url:https://fallback.example.com}")` provides a meaningful fallback. This **colon syntax** is the difference between an application that explodes on missing configuration and one that degrades gracefully.

But `@Value` has a deeper scaling problem beyond defaults. It works fine for one or two properties, but past three related values — a URL, a timeout, a retry count — it becomes scattered and untestable. Each property is injected independently, validated nowhere, and documented nowhere. For structured configuration, `@ConfigurationProperties` is the proper tool: it binds a prefix to a POJO, validates at startup, and generates IDE auto-completion metadata.

The decision is simple: **`@Value` for isolated one-off values** (a feature flag, a secret key). **`@ConfigurationProperties` for anything with a prefix and more than two properties.**

sections.title: Property Placeholders: The ${} Syntax and Its Gotchas
SpEL Expressions: The #{} Syntax for Computed Values
When @Value Stops Scaling: The Migration to @ConfigurationProperties
Key Points
sections.content:
- **No colon means startup crash** — `@Value("${api.url}")` throws `IllegalArgumentException` if `api.url` is missing; `@Value("${api.url:}")` provides an empty default. One colon is the difference.
- **Space after colon injects the space** — `${key: default}` injects `" default"` with a leading space; always write `${key:default}` without spaces or URL and numeric parsing break silently.
- **Injected once at startup, never refreshed** — `@Value` resolves at bean creation and caches the result; property changes after startup have no effect without `@RefreshScope` (Spring Cloud).
- **`${}` inside `#{}`, never reversed** — `#{'${csv.values}'.split(',')}` applies SpEL to a resolved property; the reverse nesting order is invalid.
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` for three or more related properties** — groups a prefix into a POJO with JSR-303 validation, IDE auto-completion, and `Duration`/`DataSize` auto-conversion; migrate from `@Value` when a prefix appears.
- **SpEL in `@Value` fails at startup on error** — `SpelEvaluationException` at startup if the expression fails; keep SpEL simple, move complex logic to `@PostConstruct` where you can handle errors gracefully.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Value` is the simplest way to inject external configuration — and the easiest to get wrong. A missing key crashes at startup, a space after the colon silently poisons URLs, and injected values never update without a restart.

**The `${}` syntax**
- `@Value("${key}")` looks up the key in Spring's `Environment`; if missing, throws `IllegalArgumentException` and the application will not start
- Add a default with a colon: `@Value("${key:fallback}")` — no space after the colon, or the space becomes part of the injected value
- Resolution happens once at bean creation and is cached — live reload requires `@RefreshScope` from Spring Cloud

**The `#{}` SpEL syntax**
- SpEL expressions go in `#{}`; they can call methods, reference beans, and evaluate ternary operators
- Most common pattern: `#{'${csv}'.split(',')}` — `${}` resolves the property first, SpEL transforms it; always `${}` inside `#{}`, never reversed
- If the SpEL expression fails at startup, you get `SpelEvaluationException` — keep expressions simple and move complex logic to `@PostConstruct`

When you have three or more related properties sharing a prefix, switch to `@ConfigurationProperties`. It binds the entire prefix to a POJO, validates at startup with `@Valid`, and gives your IDE auto-completion for your custom properties. `@Value` for isolated one-off values; `@ConfigurationProperties` for anything with a prefix.

steps: The ${property.key} syntax resolves against Spring's Environment, which aggregates properties from application.properties, environment variables, system properties, and command-line arguments.
Spring walks these sources in priority order and returns the first match.
Resolution happens at bean creation time, not at method call time.
The value is injected once and cached in the field.
If the property changes in the file after startup, the bean still holds the old value — there's no live reload unless you use Spring Cloud Config's @RefreshScope.

``java @Service public class PaymentClient { @Value("${payment.api.url}") private String apiUrl; @Value("${payment.timeout:5000}") private int timeoutMs; @Value("${payment.retries:3}") private int maxRetries; } ` The colon acts as a separator between the key and the default value.
